label.en: Definition 1.1 — Divisibility, Prime Factorization, and GCD / LCM
label.ar: تعريف 1.1 — Divisibility, Prime Factorization, and GCD / LCM

body.en:
Fundamental properties of integers \(\mathbb{Z}\):
  • Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: Every integer \(n > 1\) can be uniquely represented as a product of prime powers:
    \[ n = p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2} \cdot s p_k^{e_k} \]
  • GCD and LCM Product Duality: For any positive integers \(a\) and \(b\):
    \[ \gcd(a, b) \cdot \text{lcm}(a, b) = a \cdot b \]Taking prime powers \(a = \prod p_i^{a_i}\) and \(b = \prod p_i^{b_i}\):
    \[ \gcd(a, b) = \prod p_i^{\min(a_i, b_i)}, \qquad \text{lcm}(a, b) = \prod p_i^{\max(a_i, b_i)} \]
  • Divisibility Tests:
    An integer is divisible by \(3\) (or \(9\)) iff the sum of its digits is divisible by \(3\) (or \(9\)).
    An integer is divisible by \(4\) iff its last two digits form a multiple of \(4\); by \(8\) iff its last three digits form a multiple of \(8\).
    An integer is divisible by \(11\) iff the alternating sum of its digits is a multiple of \(11\).

body.en: Proportional Invariance, Linear Structure & Quantitative Modeling: Across ACT International Subject Test — Math 1, multi-step problems reduce to identifying invariant quantities—constant rates of change \(m = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\), conservation of total work/mass, or linear system rank conditions. A two-variable linear system \(a_1 x + b_1 y = c_1\), \(a_2 x + b_2 y = c_2\) has a unique intersection if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \ne \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\), no solution (parallel lines) if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \ne \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}\), and infinitely many solutions if all three ratios coincide.

label.en: Theorem 1.1 — Modular Arithmetic, Cyclicity, and Repeating Decimals
label.ar: مبرهنة 1.1 — Modular Arithmetic, Cyclicity, and Repeating Decimals

body.en:
Essential theorems for standardized exam number theory:
  • Modular Arithmetic Compatibility: If \(a \equiv c \pmod m\) and \(b \equiv d \pmod m\), then:
    \[ a + b \equiv c + d \pmod m, \qquad a \cdot b \equiv c \cdot d \pmod m, \qquad a^k \equiv c^k \pmod m \]
  • Units Digit Cyclicity: Powers of integers repeat units digits with periods dividing 4: \(2^n\) (2, 4, 8, 6), \(3^n\) (3, 9, 7, 1), \(7^n\) (7, 9, 3, 1), \(8^n\) (8, 4, 2, 6). To find the units digit of \(a^N\), compute \(N \pmod 4\).
  • Repeating Decimal to Fraction: For a repeating decimal with period \(k\):
    \[ 0.\overline{d_1 d_2 \dots d_k} = \frac{d_1 d_2 \dots d_k}{10^k - 1} = \frac{d_1 d_2 \dots d_k}{99\dots9} \]
  • Sequence Formulas:
    Arithmetic: \(a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d\), \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}(2a_1 + (n-1)d)\).
    Geometric: \(a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}\), \(S_n = \frac{a_1(1-r^n)}{1-r}\), \(S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1-r}\) for \(|r| < 1\).

label.en: ▲ ACT Math 2 Traps & Pitfalls — Number Theory
label.ar: ▲ ACT Math 2 Traps & Pitfalls — Number Theory (نظرية الأعداد المتقدمة والخصائص الحسابية)

body.en:
• Powers of \(i\) Cycle Modulo 4: \(i^1 = i\), \(i^2 = -1\), \(i^3 = -i\), and \(i^4 = 1\). To evaluate \(i^k\), find \(k \pmod 4\): remainder 1 gives \(i\), remainder 2 gives \(-1\), remainder 3 gives \(-i\), and remainder 0 gives \(1\).
  • Complex Fraction Rationalization: To simplify \(\dfrac{a+bi}{c+di}\), multiply both numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate \(c - di\). The denominator becomes the real number \(c^2 + d^2\).
  • Infinite Geometric Series Convergence: The sum formula \(S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1 - r}\) is strictly valid ONLY when |r| < 1. If \(|r| \ge 1\), the series diverges and has no finite sum.
  • GCD vs. LCM Relationship: Remember the product identity \(\text{GCD}(a,b) \times \text{LCM}(a,b) = a \times b\). If a question asks for the LCM given prime factorizations, take the highest power of each distinct prime; for GCD, take the lowest common power.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Advanced Number Theory)
label.ar: ◆ لماذا تعمل هذه الطريقة رياضياً — First-Principles اشتقاق (Advanced Number Theory)

body.en:
Why Successive Multipliers & Harmonic Average Speed Work: If a quantity \(Q_0\) undergoes a percentage change \(p\%\) followed by \(q\%\), the compound multiplier is the product of individual scale factors:

\[ Q_{\text{final}} = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\!\left(1 + \frac{q}{100}\right) = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p + q}{100} + \frac{pq}{10000}\right) \]

Notice the cross term \(\dfrac{pq}{10000}\): an increase of \(p\%\) followed by a decrease of \(p\%\) yields \(Q_0\bigl(1 - (p/100)^2\bigr) < Q_0\). Similarly, traveling equal distance \(d\) at speeds \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) takes total time \(T = \frac{d}{v_1} + \frac{d}{v_2}\), so average speed is the harmonic mean \(v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{2d}{d/v_1 + d/v_2} = \dfrac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

label.en: Worked Example — Advanced Number Theory (Medium Application)
label.ar: مثال محلول — Advanced Number Theory (Medium Application)

body.en:
Problem (Medium): For a positive integer \( k \), the greatest common divisor of \( k \) and \( 24 \) is \( 6 \), and the least common multiple of \( k \) and \( 40 \) is \( 600 \). What is the value of \( k \)?

Step-by-Step Solution: We use prime factorizations to determine the prime powers dividing \( k \). First, factor the given constants: \[ 24 = 2^3 \cdot 3^1, \quad 40 = 2^3 \cdot 5^1, \quad 600 = 2^3 \cdot 3^1 \cdot 5^2 \] From \( \text{lcm}(k, 40) = 600 \): For each prime \( p \), the exponent in the least common multiple is the maximum of the exponents in \( k \) and \( 40 \): - For \( p = 3 \): \( \max(v_3(k), 0) = 1 \implies v_3(k) = 1 \). - For \( p = 5 \): \( \max(v_5(k), 1) = 2 \implies v_5(k) = 2 \). - For \( p > 5 \): \( v_p(k) = 0 \) since no larger prime divides 600. - For \( p = 2 \): \( \max(v_2(k), 3) = 3 \implies v_2(k) \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} \). Next, use \( \gcd(k, 24) = 6 = 2^1 \cdot 3^1 \): - The power of 2 in \( \gcd(k, 24) \) is \( \min(v_2(k), 3) = 1 \), which requires \( v_2(k) = 1 \). Combining these exponents: \[ k = 2^1 \cdot 3^1 \cdot 5^2 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 25 = 150 \] Common traps: - Setting \( v_2(k) = 0 \) yields 75, but \( \gcd(75, 24) = 3 \ne 6 \). - Setting \( v_2(k) = 2 \) yields 300, but \( \gcd(300, 24) = 12 \ne 6 \).

label.en: Worked Example 1.B — Units Digit of Large Exponents via Cyclicity
label.ar: مثال محلول 1.B — Units Digit of Large Exponents via Cyclicity

body.en:
What is the units digit of \(7^{2026} + 3^{2025}\)?

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Analyze the powers of 7 modulo 10:
    \(7^1 \equiv 7\), \(7^2 \equiv 9\), \(7^3 \equiv 3\), \(7^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{10}\). Cycle length = 4.
    Divide exponent 2026 by 4:
    \[ 2026 = 4(506) + 2 \implies 7^{2026} \equiv 7^2 \equiv 9 \pmod{10} \]
  2. Analyze the powers of 3 modulo 10:
    \(3^1 \equiv 3\), \(3^2 \equiv 9\), \(3^3 \equiv 7\), \(3^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{10}\). Cycle length = 4.
    Divide exponent 2025 by 4:
    \[ 2025 = 4(506) + 1 \implies 3^{2025} \equiv 3^1 \equiv 3 \pmod{10} \]
  3. Sum the units digits:
    \[ 9 + 3 = 12 \equiv 2 \pmod{10} \]
The units digit of \(7^{2026} + 3^{2025}\) is \(\mathbf{2}\).

label.en: Worked Example \(C\) — Advanced Number Theory (Hard Application)
label.ar: مثال محلول \(C\) — Advanced Number Theory (Hard Application)

body.en:
Problem (Hard): How many ordered pairs of positive integers \((a, b)\) satisfy the equation \[ \gcd(a, b) + \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = 105? \]

Step-by-Step Solution: Let \( g = \gcd(a, b) \). Then we can express \( a = gx \) and \( b = gy \), where \( x \) and \( y \) are positive integers such that \( \gcd(x, y) = 1 \). The least common multiple is \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = gxy \). Substituting these into the given equation gives: \[ g + gxy = 105 \implies g(1 + xy) = 105 \] Since \( a, b \ge 1 \), we have \( x, y \ge 1 \), which implies \( xy \ge 1 \) and \( 1 + xy \ge 2 \). Therefore, \( g \) must be a proper positive divisor of \( 105 = 3 \times 5 \times 7 \), so \( g < 105 \). The possible values of \( g \) are \( 1, 3, 5, 7, 15, 21, 35 \). For each \( g \), we must find the number of ordered pairs \((x, y)\) of coprime positive integers such that \( xy = \frac{105}{g} - 1 \): 1. If \( g = 1 \): \( xy = 104 = 2^3 \times 13 \). The prime power factors \( 2^3 \) and \( 13 \) can each be assigned entirely to \( x \) or \( y \), yielding \( 2^2 = 4 \) coprime pairs: \( (1, 104), (8, 13), (13, 8), (104, 1) \). 2. If \( g = 3 \): \( xy = 34 = 2 \times 17 \). Distinct prime factors are 2 and 17, giving \( 2^2 = 4 \) coprime pairs: \( (1, 34), (2, 17), (17, 2), (34, 1) \). 3. If \( g = 5 \): \( xy = 20 = 2^2 \times 5 \). Prime powers \( 2^2 \) and \( 5 \) give \( 2^2 = 4 \) coprime pairs: \( (1, 20), (4, 5), (5, 4), (20, 1) \). 4. If \( g = 7 \): \( xy = 14 = 2 \times 7 \), giving \( 2^2 = 4 \) coprime pairs: \( (1, 14), (2, 7), (7, 2), (14, 1) \). 5. If \( g = 15 \): \( xy = 6 = 2 \times 3 \), giving \( 2^2 = 4 \) coprime pairs: \( (1, 6), (2, 3), (3, 2), (6, 1) \). 6. If \( g = 21 \): \( xy = 4 = 2^2 \). The only prime factor is 2. The pairs of factors of 4 are \( (1, 4), (2, 2), (4, 1) \). However, \( \gcd(2, 2) = 2 \neq 1 \), so only \( (1, 4) \) and \( (4, 1) \) are coprime. This gives \( 2 \) pairs. 7. If \( g = 35 \): \( xy = 2 \), giving \( 2 \) coprime pairs: \( (1, 2) \) and \( (2, 1) \). Since each pair \((a, b) = (gx, gy)\) uniquely determines \( g = \gcd(a, b) \), all sets of pairs across different values of \( g \) are mutually disjoint. Summing the number of pairs across all cases: \[ 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 24 \] Thus, there are 24 such ordered pairs.

label.en: Worked Example \(D\) — Advanced Number Theory (Easy Application)
label.ar: مثال محلول \(D\) — Advanced Number Theory (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): The closed interval \([12, 48]\) is shown on the number line below. How many integers \(x\) in this interval satisfy the linear congruence \[ 2x \equiv 1 \pmod 5 \text{?} \]

Step-by-Step Solution: Step 1: Solve the linear congruence \(2x \equiv 1 \pmod 5\). Since \(\gcd(2, 5) = 1\), the modular inverse of \(2\) modulo \(5\) exists. We observe that \(2 \times 3 = 6 \equiv 1 \pmod 5\), so the inverse is \(3\). Multiplying both sides by \(3\): \[ x \equiv 3 \pmod 5 \] Thus, the solutions are integers of the form \(x = 5k + 3\) for some integer \(k\). Step 2: Restrict to the closed interval \([12, 48]\): \[ 12 \le 5k + 3 \le 48 \] Subtract \(3\) from each part: \[ 9 \le 5k \le 45 \] Divide by \(5\): \[ 1.8 \le k \le 9 \] Since \(k\) must be an integer, \(k\) can take any value in the set \(\{2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\). Step 3: Count the valid integers: The number of integer values of \(k\) is \(9 - 2 + 1 = 8\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are \(13, 18, 23, 28, 33, 38, 43,\) and \(48\). A common misconception is computing \(\frac{48 - 13}{5} = 7\) and forgetting to add \(1\) for an inclusive count (fencepost error), which incorrectly leads to 7.

question.en: The sum of an arithmetic sequence is 150, with first term \(a_1 = 5\) and last term \(a_n = 25\). How many terms are in this sequence, and what is the common difference \(d\)?
question.ar: The sum of an arithmetic sequence is 150, with first term \(a_1 = 5\) and last term \(a_n = 25\). How many terms are in this sequence, and what is the common dإذا كانference \(d\)?

solution.en:
Step 1 (Find \(n\)): Use the arithmetic series sum formula:
\[ S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n) \implies 150 = \frac{n}{2}(5 + 25) = 15n \implies n = \frac{150}{15} = \mathbf{10} \]

Step 2 (Find \(d\)): Use the \(n\)-th term formula with \(n = 10\):
\[ a_{10} = a_1 + 9d \implies 25 = 5 + 9d \implies 9d = 20 \implies d = \mathbf{\frac{20}{9}} \]

question.en: Express the complex number \(z = \dfrac{5 + 2i}{3 - 4i}\) in standard form \(a + bi\), and determine its modulus \(|z|\).
question.ar: Express the complex number \(z = \dfrac{5 + 2i}{3 - 4i}\) in standard form \(a + bi\), and حدّد its modulus \(|z|\).

solution.en:
(a) Standard form \(a + bi\): Multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate \(3 + 4i\):
\[ z = \dfrac{(5 + 2i)(3 + 4i)}{(3 - 4i)(3 + 4i)} = \dfrac{15 + 20i + 6i + 8i^2}{3^2 - (4i)^2} = \dfrac{15 + 26i - 8}{9 - (-16)} = \dfrac{7 + 26i}{25} = \mathbf{\frac{7}{25} + \frac{26}{25}i} \]

(b) Modulus \(|z|\): Using the quotient property \(|z_1/z_2| = |z_1|/|z_2|\):
\[ |5 + 2i| = \sqrt{5^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{29}, \qquad |3 - 4i| = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \]\[ |z| = \mathbf{\frac{\sqrt{29}}{5}} \approx 1.077 \]

question.en: Convert the repeating decimal \(x = 0.4\overline{36} = 0.4363636\dots\) into an irreducible rational fraction \(\frac{p}{q}\).
question.ar: حل المسألة التالية في (Advanced Number Theory): Convert the repeating decimal \(x = 0.4\overline{36} = 0.4363636\dots\) into an irreducible rational fraction \(\frac{p}{q}\).

solution.en:
Let \(x = 0.4\overline{36}\). Multiply by powers of 10 to shift the non-repeating and repeating parts:
\[ 10x = 4.\overline{36} \]\[ 1000x = 436.\overline{36} \]
Subtract the first equation from the second to eliminate the repeating tails:
\[ 1000x - 10x = 436.\overline{36} - 4.\overline{36} \implies 990x = 432 \]\[ x = \frac{432}{990} \]
Divide numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor (18):
\[ 432 \div 18 = 24, \qquad 990 \div 18 = 55 \implies x = \mathbf{\frac{24}{55}} \]

\[ 1000x - 10x = 436.\overline{36} - 4.\overline{36} \implies 990x = 432 \]\[ x = \frac{432}{990} \]

\[ 432 \div 18 = 24, \qquad 990 \div 18 = 55 \implies x = \mathbf{\frac{24}{55}} \]

question.en: An infinite geometric series has first term \(a_1 = 36\) and converges to \(S_\infty = 48\). What is the common ratio \(r\), and what is the third term \(a_3\)?
question.ar: حل المسألة التالية في (Advanced Number Theory): An infinite geometric series has first term \(a_1 = 36\) and converges to \(S_\infty = 48\). What is the common ratio \(r\), and what is the third term \(a_3\)?

solution.en:
Using the infinite geometric sum formula \(S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r}\):
\[ 48 = \frac{36}{1 - r} \implies 1 - r = \frac{36}{48} = \frac{3}{4} \implies r = 1 - \frac{3}{4} = \mathbf{\frac{1}{4}} \]
Since \(|r| = \frac{1}{4} < 1\), the convergence condition holds.
Find the third term \(a_3 = a_1 r^2\):
\[ a_3 = 36 \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2 = 36 \times \frac{1}{16} = \mathbf{\frac{9}{4}} = 2.25 \]

\[ 48 = \frac{36}{1 - r} \implies 1 - r = \frac{36}{48} = \frac{3}{4} \implies r = 1 - \frac{3}{4} = \mathbf{\frac{1}{4}} \]
Since \(|r| = \frac{1}{4} < 1\), the convergence condition holds.

question.en: What is the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( 126n \) is the square of an integer?
question.ar: حل المسألة التالية في (Advanced Number Theory): What is the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( 126n \) is the square of an integer?

hints.en: To find the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( 126n \) is a perfect square, first find the prime factorization of 126: \(126 = 2 \times 63 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7\).
hints.ar: To أوجد smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( 126n \) is a perfect square, first أوجد prime حلّلization of 126: \(126 = 2 \times 63 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7\).

hints.en: For an integer to be a perfect square, every prime factor in its prime factorization must have an even exponent. In the prime factorization of 126: - The factor 2 has an exponent of 1 (odd).
hints.ar: For an integer to be a perfect square, every prime حلّل in its prime حلّلization must have an even exponent. In the prime حلّلization of 126: - The حلّل 2 has an exponent of 1 (odd).

hints.en: Then \(126 \times 14 = 1764\), which is a perfect square.
hints.ar: تلميح للحل: استخدم العلاقة \(126 \times 14 = 1764\) لتبسيط الخطوة.

solution.en:
To find the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( 126n \) is a perfect square, first find the prime factorization of 126:
\[ 126 = 2 \times 63 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7 \]
For an integer to be a perfect square, every prime factor in its prime factorization must have an even exponent.

In the prime factorization of 126:
- The factor 2 has an exponent of 1 (odd).
- The factor 3 has an exponent of 2 (even).
- The factor 7 has an exponent of 1 (odd).

To make all exponents even with the smallest positive integer \( n \), \( n \) must provide at least one factor of 2 and one factor of 7:
\[ n = 2^1 \times 7^1 = 14 \]
Then \( 126 \times 14 = 1764 = 42^2 \), which is a perfect square.

Common misconceptions:
- Choosing 7 only pairs the factor 7, leaving 2 with an odd exponent (\( 126 \times 7 = 882 \), not a square).
- Choosing 21 multiplies by \( 3 \times 7 \), leaving 2 unpaired.
- Choosing 42 gives \( 126 \times 42 = 5292 \), which is not a square and is greater than 14.
solution.ar:
To أوجد smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( 126n \) is a perfect square, first أوجد prime حلّلization of 126:
\[ 126 = 2 \times 63 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7 \]
For an integer to be a perfect square, every prime حلّل in its prime حلّلization must have an even exponent.

In the prime حلّلization of 126:
- The حلّل 2 has an exponent of 1 (odd).
- The حلّل 3 has an exponent of 2 (even).
- The حلّل 7 has an exponent of 1 (odd).

To make all exponents even with the smallest positive integer \( n \), \( n \) must provide at least one حلّل of 2 and one حلّل of 7:
\[ n = 2^1 \times 7^1 = 14 \]
Then \( 126 \times 14 = 1764 = 42^2 \), which is a perfect square.

Common misconceptions:
- Choosing 7 only pairs the حلّل 7, leaving 2 with an odd exponent (\( 126 \times 7 = 882 \), not a square).
- Choosing 21 multiplies by \( 3 \times 7 \), leaving 2 unpaired.
- Choosing 42 gives \( 126 \times 42 = 5292 \), which is not a square and is greater than 14.
